summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets, concurrency needs, streaming support, and whether Hosted, Dedicated or Private options fit LucidCart's e-commerce realtime personalization use case. Main asks: 100ms-300ms p95 depending on model size, burst concurrency to 200, streaming for token-at-a-time product descriptions, and data residency/KMS concerns. Agreed next steps: share benchmarks, pricing, and set POC kickoff.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-05-07
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Tom Alvarez (LucidCart CTO), Priya Singh (ML Eng), Daniel Cho (Infra)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and I'm here with Jordan our SE, we'll run through a couple quick questions about latency and throughput and what LucidCart is trying to achieve.
[00:12] Tom: Hi Maya, hi Jordan, thanks, appreciate it. We're hoping to understand if Redwood Hosted can hit our p95 targets, or if we need Dedicated, or even Private for some customers.
[00:22] Jordan: Great, and just to set expectations, we'll ask about your traffic patterns, p95 goals, model families, and then share some benchmarking guidance.
[00:30] Priya: Quick context — we run a personalized product description generator, average prompt ~120 tokens, responses ~220 tokens, and we need streaming token-by-token output to show progressive text in the UI.
[00:44] Daniel: Our peak concurrent sessions are about 120 active users hitting the generator, but we need to plan for bursts up to ~200 concurrency for promo events.
[00:56] Maya: Helpful. What are your p95 latency targets today?
[01:03] Tom: We want p95 in the 200–300ms range for the smaller models used in A/B tests, and up to 800–1,000ms for larger ones, but the smaller models are the blocking ones for UX.
[01:18] Jordan: Okay, 200–300ms p95 on small-ish models is tight but feasible depending on topology — e.g., sequence length, quantized model, and whether you have prefix caching enabled.
[01:30] Priya: When you say prefix caching, do you mean the KV cache — we've heard Redwood does automatic prefix/KV cache?
[01:38] Jordan: Yes, automatic prefix and KV cache; apologies, auto-transcript might say KV cash sometimes — but we do keep key-value cache in memory across requests which can drastically reduce token generation latency for repeated contexts.
[01:50] Tom: For our streaming use case, we need token/sec throughput too — something like 200 tokens/sec sustained per instance or per call? How do you usually measure that?
[02:03] Jordan: We measure both per-request token/sec and aggregate tokens/sec across the fleet. For streaming it's often about per-call tail latency and how the runtime pipelines token generation and network streaming.
[02:16] Maya: Maybe helpful to surface typical baseline numbers: on an 80B-ish model on high-end GPUs, you might see X tokens/sec in q4 quantized mode, smaller models are much faster. We'll share concrete numbers in the spreadsheet.
[02:30] Priya: Understood. Also, what's the concurrency model — if we have 200 concurrent streaming calls, does Redwood do continuous batching that would hurt streaming latency?
[02:42] Jordan: Continuous batching can help throughput but we have latency-aware routing. For streaming-sensitive routes we prioritize low-latency execution with smaller batch sizes and faster kernel choices. It is a tradeoff: throughput vs p95 latency.
[02:56] Tom: For Hosted versus Dedicated — what are the hard limits? We need predictable p95 SLAs for enterprise customers.
[03:05] Maya: Hosted is for quick time-to-value and can handle a lot of scale, but Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and predictable latency/throughput. Private if you need VPC/on-prem and KMS control. Pricing and SLAs differ — we'll send the comparison.
[03:20] Daniel: And on security — we need SOC 2, SAML SSO integration, and customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). Any blockers?
[03:30] Jordan: No blockers — Hosted supports SOC 2, SSO, audit logs; Dedicated and Private provide stronger isolation and KMS options. For Private we can run a control plane in your VPC and integrate with your KMS.
[03:44] Priya: Can you speak to how fallbacks work? If a Hosted instance is overloaded would it route to a smaller model or degrade gracefully?
[03:53] Jordan: Yes, smart routing policies can fallback to compatible model variants or different regions to maintain p95 SLOs. We can configure automatic fallback to a quantized variant to keep latency low.
[04:05] Tom: About benchmarking — we want to run token/sec and p95 tests ourselves. What's the recommended methodology?
[04:12] Jordan: We recommend a two-phase approach: 1) synthetic microbenchmarks per model/config to get tokens/sec and p95 at different sequence lengths; 2) replay of real traces to measure real-world concurrency effects. We'll provide a spreadsheet and runner.
[04:28] Maya: We'll also include guidance for streaming — measure per-token latency, handshake overhead, and tail percentiles under burst.
[04:36] Priya: One more thing: are there differences in kernel selection for quantized models that could affect streaming?
[04:44] Jordan: Kernel selection and attention optimizations matter a lot. For quantized paths we pick different kernels optimized for int8 or nf4, which changes per-token execution time. For streaming we bias toward kernels minimizing per-token overhead.
[04:58] Tom: Good. For expected numbers — could you give a ballpark for p95 on a 13B and 70B model for our 120/220 token average?
[05:08] Jordan: Rough ballpark (very rough): 13B deterministic quantized path p95 synchronous maybe 150–350ms depending on batching and sequence lengths; 70B often 500–900ms. We'll put ranges in the doc.
[05:25] Maya: And another practical item, if you need reserved throughput for a campaign we can propose Dedicated capacity with autoscaling policies and burst buckets.
[05:34] Daniel: That burst bucket concept — can we pre-provision a burst of N tokens/sec for 10 minutes?
[05:40] Jordan: Yes, we support configurable burst capacity and policies — e.g., maintain base throughput and allow short bursts within a quota.
[05:49] Priya: For telemetry, we need per-route token and latency breakdowns, and traces correlated to user requests. Does Redwood surface token-level cost?
[05:58] Maya: Yes, Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns and per-route dashboards. We also have tracing hooks for request-level debugging.
[06:08] Tom: Ok, good. On the topic of model versions and rollouts — if we do canary for a new quantization profile, can Redwood automatically rollback on quality regressions?
[06:17] Jordan: Yes, rollouts support canary/A-B and automatic fallback policies if evals or quality monitoring detect regressions tied to prompt sets.
[06:26] Priya: For the POC we'd want to benchmark using our real traffic shape. We'll provide a day of traces covering normal and peak traffic.
[06:34] Maya: Perfect. We'll also include a lightweight runner that simulates streaming clients hitting the endpoint to measure end-to-end p95.
[06:44] Tom: Are there any gotchas about VPC egress for streaming that increase latency?
[06:50] Jordan: Network egress and region placement matter. For Private deployments within your VPC, network hops are minimal. For Hosted, placing in a nearby region and optimizing egress paths reduces added latency.
[07:02] Speaker 1: (murmur)
[07:08] Tom: For contract timing — if we like the POC results we want to move to Dedicated within 6-8 weeks.
[07:14] Maya: That's reasonable. We'll outline timelines in the next email.
[07:19] Priya: One operational Q: do you maintain per-session KV cache affinity? For personalization we often reuse user history, so cache affinity could help reduce cold-start latency.
[07:29] Jordan: We can pin sessions to warm KV caches, yes. There's tradeoffs around memory and eviction policies but it's supported.
[07:38] Daniel: Regarding monitoring, we want alerting on p95 regressions and token surge anomalies. Is alerting built into the Console or do we wire to PagerDuty?
[07:47] Maya: Console has built-in alerting and you can forward to external systems like PagerDuty. We'll share an example alerts playbook.
[07:56] Tom: Switching back to numbers, you said you'll provide token/sec baselines. For our 120/220 token case, what's the recommended concurrency draft for target 250ms p95 on the small models?
[08:08] Jordan: If you want 250ms p95, try to keep per-instance concurrency low — e.g., 8–16 concurrent streams per GPU for small quantized models, combined with multiple instances behind a routing policy. But we'll help tune exact numbers during the POC.
[08:22] Priya: Would warm caching reduce concurrency needs?
[08:25] Jordan: Yes, reuse of KV cache and prefix caching can reduce overall token work and improve p95.
[08:32] [09:10] (skipping ahead, mid-call details and interruptions)
[09:15] Maya: Quick question — are there any sensitive customer data flows we should be aware of when running Hosted POC?
[09:22] Tom: We have PII in product descriptions rarely, and some customer IDs. We want data not to be used for model training and to have retention settings.
[09:31] Jordan: Hosted supports data controls — retention settings, no-training guarantees for enterprise, and we can enable encryption in transit and at rest. For max control Dedicated/Private are options.
[09:45] Priya: About SSO — we use Okta; what's the SAML integration cadence?
[09:52] Maya: We support SAML/SSO with Okta and can do a configuration guide.
[09:58] Daniel: Any limit on streaming payload size? We sometimes send larger JSON wrappers with metadata.
[10:04] Jordan: No hard limit beyond request size quotas; we'll share recommended payload sizes and advise on compressing metadata.
[10:12] Tom: Let's talk failure modes — if a node goes down during streaming, do you have resume semantics?
[10:20] Jordan: Not native per-token resume across nodes currently; we typically fail the request and route the retry. But we can design a schema to stream fragments and reassemble in-app.
[10:32] Priya: Ok, we'll account for that.
[10:35] Maya: Wrapping up capability questions — is there a recommended way to evaluate latency vs cost for model selection?
[10:43] Jordan: Yes, Redwood Optimize provides model/quantization recommendations by workload and a cost/latency tradeoff analysis. We'll include some initial recommendations for your prompts.
[10:56] Tom: Great. For the POC acceptance criteria, we'll want: p95 below 300ms for the small model at 150 concurrent users, streaming correctness preserved, and an ops runbook.
[11:09] Maya: Noted — we'll propose a POC acceptance criteria doc in the next email.
[11:16] Daniel: One final network question — can Dedicated be colocated in our cloud account or is it always managed by Redwood?
[11:24] Maya: Dedicated is managed by Redwood but can be isolated in a VPC with network peering or Private Link. Private deployment is the one where the control plane runs in your account.
[11:36] Priya: Are there any measurable differences in p95 between Dedicated and Private beyond network hops?
[11:43] Jordan: Mostly network and control-plane placement. If the Private deployment is on-prem there may be hardware differences; otherwise Dedicated with reserved GPUs gives similar predictability.
[11:55] Tom: Okay, let's talk timeline and next steps.
[12:00] Maya: We'll send pricing and the benchmarking spreadsheet today, Jordan will follow up with the runner and recommended prompts, and you will share traces. Then we'll schedule the POC kickoff.
[12:10] Tom: Sounds good. Thank you both.
[12:14] (call winds down, pleasantries)

[33:00] Jordan: (after deep technical dive later in call) We did a quick sketch — if you want 200 concurrency sustaining streaming at 50 tokens/sec per session, the aggregate token/sec demand becomes quite high and you likely need Dedicated capacity. We'll attach an example capacity calc.
[34:20] Priya: For that calc could you show the break down per GPU type?
[34:28] Jordan: Yes, we'll include GPU-level throughput numbers and the kernel choices per model.
[36:01] Daniel: Re: KV cache eviction — what are common settings?
[36:08] Jordan: LRU with configurable window, but for personalization we recommend affinity-based warm caches.
[38:30] Tom: Any final concerns from Redwood side about our PII handling in Hosted?
[38:38] Maya: We'll include our data handling document; for strict requirements consider Private.
[40:05] Priya: One last small point — can Redwood's Console export detailed per-route token logs for billing reconciliation?
[40:13] Maya: Yes, exportable logs and we can provide sample CSVs.
[42:00] Tom: Ok, let's finalize — we'll aim to send traces by 2026-05-14 and book the POC kickoff for week of 2026-05-18.
[42:12] Maya: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the items.
[46:00] (meeting ends)
